q: A guest brings their own bottle and the restaurant adds a fee. What is that fee called?
opts: A fee for serving wine a guest has brought
A charge for opening any bottle on the list
exp: It covers glassware, service and the lost sale, and it applies only to the bottle the guest carried in. Policies vary widely and are worth stating plainly on the list.

q: Within a meal, wines are conventionally sequenced how?
opts: Light before heavy, dry before sweet
Heavier before lighter, so the palate is opened early
Sweet before dry, to clear the palate first
exp: Young before old as well. Each wine should not be diminished by the one before it, and the rule bends for a deliberate contrast, knowingly.

q: Recommending a wine well within a guest's stated budget achieves what?
opts: It reduces the bill and costs the room a returning guest
It builds trust and usually returns more over time
exp: Selling to the budget rather than above it is the durable strategy. A guest who feels handled does not come back.

q: A bottle says Cabernet Sauvignon on the front label. Under federal rules, how much of that grape must be in the wine?
exp: Federal law sets the varietal floor at 75 percent, so a quarter of the blend can be something else entirely. Several states, Oregon among them, hold their producers to a stricter figure.

q: A petition to draw the boundaries of a new American wine region is filed with which body?
opts: The Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau
exp: The TTB, part of the Treasury, evaluates the evidence for a distinctive growing area and grants the AVA. Petitions are usually brought by the growers themselves rather than by any government body.

q: A grower inside an AVA plants whatever variety he likes at whatever yield he likes and still puts the AVA name on the label. Why is that permitted?
opts: He holds a federal exemption from the AVA rules
AVA rules govern yield but leave grape choice open
AVA rules bind only wineries that own more than fifty acres
An AVA fixes boundaries and sets no rule on grape or yield
exp: This is the central difference from a European appellation, which typically dictates permitted varieties, maximum yields and often winemaking. An AVA sets no rule at all on which grape is planted or how heavily it is cropped; it is a statement about place and nothing else.

q: For a wine carrying an AVA on its label, a stated vintage must account for at least how much of the fruit?
exp: The figure is 95 percent for an AVA, but only 85 percent when the appellation given is a state or a county. The tighter the place claim, the tighter the vintage rule.

q: The words Estate Bottled appear across the bottom of a label. What does that guarantee?
opts: The wine was bottled by hand rather than on a line
The estate has been in the same family for at least fifty years
The wine came from one single vineyard, wherever the winery happens to sit
The winery sits inside the named AVA and grew, made and bottled the wine there
exp: Estate Bottled is one of the few American label terms with real legal weight: the fruit has to come off land the winery owns or controls inside that same AVA, and the wine must be crushed, aged and bottled on the premises. Reserve, by contrast, means whatever the producer wants it to mean.

q: Which state can claim the very first AVA ever approved, granted in 1980?
exp: Augusta, on the Missouri River, was approved months ahead of Napa Valley. Missouri had a large and serious wine industry in the nineteenth century, which is easy to forget now.

q: A label reads Russian River Valley. At minimum, how much of the fruit came from inside those boundaries?
exp: An AVA name requires 85 percent, while federal law asks only 75 percent for a county or state name. California is stricter than that federal floor, so a Sonoma County wine needs 75 percent Sonoma fruit but must be 100 percent California grown.

q: At a 1976 tasting in Paris a California red finished ahead of the Bordeaux field. Which producer made it?
exp: Stag's Leap Wine Cellars took the red flight and Chateau Montelena the white, both with 1973s. The result did more for California's international standing than any amount of marketing could have.

q: More Napa acreage goes to one variety than to any other. Which is it?
exp: Cabernet Sauvignon takes roughly half of Napa's planted area and drives its reputation and its prices. Chardonnay is a distant second.

q: Cool air off San Pablo Bay reaches the southern end of the valley. Which pair of grapes does that suit?
exp: Los Carneros straddles the Napa and Sonoma county line at the water's edge and is cold by Napa standards. Much of California's better sparkling base wine comes from there.

q: A Napa vineyard planted high enough to sit clear of the fog that fills the valley below is most likely in which AVA?
exp: Howell Mountain vineyards must lie above 1,400 feet, which puts them above the fog line. Mountain fruit tends to be smaller berried and more tannic than fruit from the valley floor.

q: Which pair of appellations sit side by side on the valley floor immediately north of Yountville?
exp: The Oakville and Rutherford benches are gravelly, well drained alluvial fans and form the historic heartland of Napa Cabernet. Rutherford dust is the old shorthand for the dusty tannin found there.

q: In 1968 Napa County passed a measure that has shaped the valley ever since. What did it do?
opts: It required all Napa wine to be estate bottled
It banned irrigation on the valley floor
It capped yields for every vineyard in the county
It zoned the valley floor for agriculture
exp: The Agricultural Preserve was the first of its kind in the country and set a large minimum parcel size, which blocked subdivision of the valley floor. Without it the valley floor would very likely be housing today.
